source.title: Analysis of Lower Extremity Contraction According to Gender Using Tensiomyography

paper.citation: Kim, B.-K., Chai, J.-H., Kim, C., Kim, C.-H., & Bae, S.-W. (2017). Analysis of lower extremity contraction according to gender using tensiomyography. The Korean Journal of Sports Medicine, 35(3), 181–189. https://doi.org/10.5763/kjsm.2017.35.3.181
paper.abstract: Do maximal radial displacement, contraction time, and calculated contraction velocity differ between healthy male and female university students across selected quadriceps and hamstring muscles? Participants: 15 male and 12 female university students without orthopedic disease; men were 22.27 ± 4.25 years and women 21.58 ± 1.73 years. Sport and level: Healthy university students; athlete status and sport were not reported. Training or return-to-play context: Resting lower-extremity muscle-characteristic assessment. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Physically active young adults without orthopedic disease; measurements were not linked to injury, performance, or longitudinal adaptation. Design: Cross-sectional sex-group comparison. Exposure or intervention: Electrically evoked tensiomyography of bilateral rectus femoris, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, biceps femoris, and semitendinosus. Comparator: Male versus female participant groups. Measurements and outcomes: Maximal displacement (Dm), contraction time (Tc), and contraction velocity calculated as Dm × 0.8 / Tc. Analysis: Participants avoided strenuous exercise, alcohol, and caffeine for 24 hours and rested supine for at least five minutes; independent t tests or Mann–Whitney U tests were used as appropriate with alpha 0.05.
paper.tldr: This study informs interpretation of tensiomyography by showing that reference values may differ between young adult male and female groups and across specific thigh muscles. Bilateral summed vastus medialis Dm was higher in men than women (16.18 ± 3.00 versus 11.98 ± 2.62 mm, p = 0.001). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Cross-sectional sex-group comparison. Exposure or intervention: Electrically evoked tensiomyography of bilateral rectus femoris, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, biceps femoris, and semitendinosus. Comparator: Male versus female participant groups. Measurements and outcomes: Maximal displacement (Dm), contraction time (Tc), and contraction velocity calculated as Dm × 0.8 / Tc. Analysis: Participants avoided strenuous exercise, alcohol, and caffeine for 24 hours and rested supine for at least five minutes; independent t tests or Mann–Whitney U tests were used as appropriate with alpha 0.05.
paper.findings: Bilateral summed vastus medialis Dm was higher in men than women (16.18 ± 3.00 versus 11.98 ± 2.62 mm, p = 0.001). Bilateral summed biceps femoris Dm was lower in men than women (15.14 ± 4.93 versus 20.47 ± 3.48 mm, p = 0.001). Bilateral summed biceps femoris Tc was longer in men than women (97.77 ± 26.90 versus 70.20 ± 12.53 ms, p = 0.002). Bilateral summed contraction velocity differed for vastus medialis (men 0.58 ± 0.11 versus women 0.41 ± 0.11 mm/ms, p = 0.001) and biceps femoris (men 0.27 ± 0.10 versus women 0.46 ± 0.09 mm/ms, p < 0.001).
paper.limitations: The sample was small, young, and drawn from male and female students at different universities; sport, training history, body composition, menstrual status, and habitual activity were not reported. The cross-sectional design cannot determine whether differences arose from sex, anthropometry, training exposure, muscle architecture, or another confounder. Physiological interpretations of Dm, Tc, and calculated velocity were indirect; muscle stiffness, hypertrophy, fiber type, and force were not measured concurrently. Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): these group means should not be used as diagnostic thresholds for injury or readiness and do not establish how collegiate athletes should be compared or monitored.
paper.practicalImplications: When using TMG, compare an athlete against a standardized personal baseline and interpret each muscle separately. Sex-group reference values may provide context, but body size, training history, electrode/sensor placement, joint position, stimulation protocol, and measurement error need to be controlled before attributing a difference to physiology or injury.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. When using TMG, compare an athlete against a standardized personal baseline and interpret each muscle separately. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, when using TMG, compare an athlete against a standardized personal baseline and interpret each muscle separately. Sex-group reference values may provide context, but body size, training history, electrode/sensor placement, joint position, stimulation protocol, and measurement error need to be controlled before attributing a difference to physiology or injury. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
